why: ISO 27001 is the standard named most often in French and European GRC offers, and many junior GRC consultants start on ISO 27001 projects: gap assessments, Statements of Applicability, internal audits and certification preparation. Interviews go into the details: the clauses, Annex A, the mandatory documents and how a certification audit works.
outcome: explain what an ISMS is and how ISO 27001:2022 is structured, define the scope and roles, run the risk assessment and treatment the standard requires, write a Statement of Applicability, navigate the 93 Annex A controls, list the mandatory documented information, plan and run an internal audit, write nonconformities and corrective actions, and prepare an organisation for the stage 1 and stage 2 certification audits.

lessons.title: What ISO 27001 is and how it is built
text: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard for an information security management system, or ISMS (SMSI in French). An ISMS is not a tool or a firewall: it is the set of policies, processes, roles, risk assessments and controls by which an organisation manages information security in a structured way and keeps improving it. The standard says what the system must achieve, not which products to buy, so it fits a 20-person start-up as well as a bank.

The current version is ISO/IEC 27001:2022, amended in 2024 to mention climate change in the context clauses. Organisations certified against the 2013 version had until 31 October 2025 to move to the 2022 version. The standard has two parts. Clauses 4 to 10 describe the management system itself and are mandatory for certification. Annex A lists 93 information security controls that the organisation must consider and either apply or justify excluding.

Clauses 4 to 10 follow the same structure as other ISO management system standards such as ISO 9001 for quality: 4 context of the organisation, 5 leadership, 6 planning, 7 support, 8 operation, 9 performance evaluation and 10 improvement. They follow the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle: plan the ISMS from the context and the risks, implement the controls, check with measurement, audits and management review, and act on the findings to improve.

ISO/IEC 27002 is the companion guide: for each Annex A control it explains the purpose and gives implementation guidance. Organisations are not certified against 27002, but auditors and implementers read it constantly. Other standards of the family include ISO 27005 for risk management, ISO 27017 and 27018 for cloud services and personal data in the cloud, and ISO 27701 for a privacy information management system.

Why companies get certified: clients and tenders require it, it gives a structured way to meet obligations such as NIS2 and GDPR security requirements, and it shows management and partners that security is governed, not improvised. A certificate covers a defined scope only, which is why reading the scope is the first thing to do when a supplier sends one.
points: ISMS: the policies, processes, roles, risk assessments and controls that manage security and improve it.
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (amended 2024); transition from the 2013 version ended on 31 October 2025.
Clauses 4-10 (mandatory management system) + Annex A (93 controls to consider).
Plan-Do-Check-Act; same structure as ISO 9001 and other management system standards.
ISO 27002: guidance on each control; certification is against 27001 only, for a defined scope.

lessons.title: Context, scope and leadership (clauses 4 and 5)
text: Clause 4 asks the organisation to understand itself before securing anything. It identifies internal and external issues that affect information security: its strategy, its IT, the threat landscape, laws, and since the 2024 amendment, whether climate change is relevant. It lists the interested parties (clients, regulators, staff, shareholders, suppliers) and their requirements, and decides which of these requirements the ISMS will address.

Then comes the scope: which parts of the organisation, which sites, which services, which systems are inside the ISMS, and the interfaces and dependencies with what is outside. The scope must be documented. A narrow scope (one SaaS product and its team) makes certification faster, but clients will check whether it covers the service they buy; a scope that excludes an essential dependency, such as the data centre run by another team, will not convince an auditor.

Clause 5 is about leadership. Top management must show commitment: approve the information security policy, make sure the ISMS has resources, integrate security into business processes, and communicate why it matters. Auditors interview management and look for real evidence such as minutes of management review, budget decisions and signed policies; a CISO acting alone without management involvement is a classic weakness.

The information security policy required by clause 5.2 is a short document that fits the purpose of the organisation, sets or frames the security objectives, commits to meeting applicable requirements and to continual improvement, and is communicated and available. Topic-specific policies (access control, supplier security, backup and so on) come from Annex A.

Finally, roles and responsibilities are assigned and communicated, including who is responsible for making sure the ISMS conforms to the standard and who reports on its performance to management. In practice: an ISMS manager or CISO, risk owners, control owners, and a security committee where management takes decisions.
points: 4.1 internal and external issues (including climate change since 2024); 4.2 interested parties and their requirements.
4.3 documented scope: units, sites, services, systems, interfaces and dependencies.
5.1 management commitment, shown with evidence (reviews, budget, decisions).
5.2 information security policy: fits the purpose, frames objectives, commits to requirements and improvement.
5.3 roles and responsibilities: ISMS manager, risk owners, control owners, security committee.

ISMS scope (example)
The information security management system covers the design, development,
hosting and support of the "PayFlow" SaaS platform, operated from the Lyon
office, with production hosted at the cloud provider's Paris region.
Included: product, engineering, support and IT teams; production and
development environments; the laptops and SaaS tools they use.
Interfaces: HR (onboarding, payroll) and finance remain outside the scope
and are covered by service agreements with the ISMS.

lessons.title: Planning: risks, treatment and the Statement of Applicability (clause 6)
text: Clause 6 is the heart of the standard. The organisation defines and applies an information security risk assessment process: criteria for accepting risks and for performing assessments, so that repeated assessments give consistent, valid and comparable results. It identifies risks to confidentiality, integrity and availability within the scope, names a risk owner for each, analyses their likelihood and consequences, and evaluates them against the criteria. ISO 27001 does not impose a method: ISO 27005, EBIOS RM or a home-made method are all fine if they meet these requirements.

Next, the risk treatment process: choose treatment options, determine the controls needed, and compare them with Annex A to check that no necessary control has been forgotten. The result is a risk treatment plan, approved by the risk owners, who also accept the residual risks. Auditors check that the link between risks and controls is real: each control should be justified by a risk, a requirement or a contract.

The Statement of Applicability (SoA) is a mandatory document that lists every Annex A control, says whether it is applicable, justifies the inclusion or exclusion, and states whether it is implemented. It may also list additional controls that are not in Annex A. The SoA is the document auditors ask for first, and clients often ask to see it too. An exclusion needs a real reason: “7.4 Physical security monitoring not applicable: we have no office of our own, staff work remotely and the data centre is the cloud provider’s, covered by its certifications” is acceptable; “not needed” is not.

Clause 6.2 asks for information security objectives: measurable where possible, consistent with the policy, monitored, communicated and updated, with a plan saying what will be done, by whom, with which resources, by when and how results will be evaluated. Example: “100 % of administrator accounts with MFA by the end of Q2” or “critical vulnerabilities fixed within 14 days in 90 % of cases”.

Clause 6.3, added in 2022, asks that changes to the ISMS itself be planned rather than improvised. Together, these elements make clause 6 the place where the ISMS becomes specific to the organisation: two companies certified to ISO 27001 can have very different controls, because they have different risks.
points: 6.1.2 risk assessment process with acceptance criteria, consistent results, risk owners; method free.
6.1.3 risk treatment: choose options, determine controls, compare with Annex A, plan approved by risk owners.
Statement of Applicability: every Annex A control, applicable or not, justification, implementation status.
6.2 measurable security objectives with a plan (what, who, resources, when, how evaluated).
6.3 changes to the ISMS are planned.

lessons.title: Annex A: the 93 controls
text: Annex A of ISO 27001:2022 groups 93 controls in four themes. Organisational controls (5.1 to 5.37) cover policies, roles, segregation of duties, threat intelligence, asset inventory, information classification, access control and identity management, supplier relationships and cloud services, incident management, business continuity, legal requirements, privacy and independent review. People controls (6.1 to 6.8) cover screening, terms of employment, awareness and training, the disciplinary process, responsibilities after leaving, confidentiality agreements, remote working and event reporting.

Physical controls (7.1 to 7.14) cover security perimeters, entry, offices and rooms, physical monitoring, protection against environmental threats, working in secure areas, clear desk and clear screen, equipment siting, assets off-premises, storage media, supporting utilities, cabling, maintenance and secure disposal. Technological controls (8.1 to 8.34) cover endpoints, privileged access, authentication, malware, vulnerabilities, configuration, deletion and masking of data, data leakage prevention, backup, redundancy, logging and monitoring, clock synchronisation, network security, cryptography, secure development, testing, separation of environments and change management.

The 2022 revision merged and reorganised the 114 controls of the 2013 version into 93, and added 11 new ones: threat intelligence (5.7), information security for the use of cloud services (5.23), ICT readiness for business continuity (5.30), physical security monitoring (7.4), configuration management (8.9), information deletion (8.10), data masking (8.11), data leakage prevention (8.12), monitoring activities (8.16), web filtering (8.23) and secure coding (8.28). Interviewers like to ask for a few of them.

ISO 27002:2022 gives each control attributes that help to filter and map them: control type (preventive, detective, corrective), the information security properties protected (confidentiality, integrity, availability), cybersecurity concepts aligned with the NIST CSF functions (identify, protect, detect, respond, recover), operational capabilities and security domains. These attributes make mapping to other frameworks easier.

Annex A is a checklist to make sure nothing important is forgotten, not a list to apply blindly. Some controls will be excluded with a justification, and the way each control is implemented depends on the risks: “8.5 Secure authentication” can mean passwords plus MFA for a small company, and smart cards and privileged access workstations for a bank.
points: Organisational 5.1-5.37 (37), people 6.1-6.8 (8), physical 7.1-7.14 (14), technological 8.1-8.34 (34) = 93.
2013 → 2022: 114 controls reorganised into 93, with 11 new ones.

New: 5.7 threat intelligence, 5.23 cloud services, 5.30 ICT continuity, 7.4 physical monitoring, 8.9 configuration, 8.10 deletion, 8.11 masking, 8.12 DLP, 8.16 monitoring, 8.23 web filtering, 8.28 secure coding.
ISO 27002 attributes: control type, CIA properties, cybersecurity concepts, capabilities, domains.
Annex A is a completeness check; implementation depends on the risks.

lessons.title: Support, operation and documented information (clauses 7 and 8)
text: Clause 7 covers what the ISMS needs to work. Resources: people, time and budget. Competence: the people who affect security have the skills needed, and the organisation keeps evidence of it (training records, certifications, experience). Awareness: everyone knows the policy, how they contribute and what happens if they do not follow it. Communication: what is communicated, when, to whom and by whom, internally and externally, for example to clients during an incident.

Documented information is the standard’s term for documents and records. The organisation keeps the documented information the standard requires and the information it decides is needed for its ISMS to be effective. Documents must be identified (title, version, owner, date), reviewed and approved, available where needed, protected and kept under change control. Records must not be altered.

The documents and records an auditor expects as a minimum are: the scope, the information security policy, the risk assessment and treatment processes, the Statement of Applicability, the risk treatment plan, the security objectives, evidence of competence, the documentation needed to operate the processes, the results of risk assessments and treatments, monitoring and measurement results, the internal audit programme and results, the management review results, and the nonconformities with their corrective actions. Annex A controls add others, such as the asset inventory, the access control policy and the incident procedure.

Clause 8 is about running the plan: operating the processes and controls as planned, controlling changes and externally provided processes, performing risk assessments at planned intervals and when significant changes occur, implementing the risk treatment plan, and keeping the results. Auditors test this by sampling: the last two risk assessment updates, the changes made in the last quarter, the supplier reviews of the year.

A common mistake is to write documents for the auditor rather than for the people who use them. A 60-page procedure no one follows produces nonconformities; a two-page procedure that matches what people really do, with records proving it, produces a calm audit.
points: 7.1 resources, 7.2 competence with evidence, 7.3 awareness, 7.4 communication plan.
7.5 documented information: identified, approved, available, protected, under change control.
Minimum set: scope, policy, risk processes, SoA, treatment plan, objectives, competence, results, audit programme, management review, nonconformities.
Clause 8: operate as planned, control changes and suppliers, reassess risks, implement the treatment plan.
Write documents for the people who use them; keep records that prove the process runs.

lessons.title: Measuring, internal audit and improvement (clauses 9 and 10)
text: Clause 9.1 asks the organisation to decide what to monitor and measure, with which method, when, who analyses the results and when. Typical measures are the indicators seen in the security committee: patching within targets, access reviews completed, training completion, incidents by severity, objectives achieved. The point is to evaluate the performance and effectiveness of the ISMS, not to produce numbers for their own sake.

Clause 9.2 requires internal audits at planned intervals, covering the whole scope and all the clauses over the audit cycle, usually once a year. The audit programme defines the frequency, methods, responsibilities and reporting. Auditors must be objective and impartial: they do not audit their own work. ISO 19011 gives guidance on auditing management systems and ISO 27007 applies it to ISMS. An internal audit works like the certification audit: plan, opening meeting, interviews, document review, sampling of records, observation, findings, closing meeting and report.

Clause 9.3, the management review, is a meeting where top management reviews the ISMS at planned intervals. Its inputs are set by the standard: status of actions from previous reviews, changes in issues and interested parties, feedback on performance (nonconformities, monitoring results, audit results, objectives), feedback from interested parties, risk assessment results and treatment plan status, and opportunities for improvement. Its outputs are decisions on improvement and on changes to the ISMS, recorded in minutes.

Clause 10 deals with improvement. When a nonconformity occurs (a requirement not met), the organisation reacts to control and correct it, finds the root cause, checks whether similar problems exist elsewhere, takes corrective action to prevent recurrence, checks that the action worked, and keeps records. A correction fixes the case (the leaver’s account is disabled); a corrective action removes the cause (account disabling is automated from the HR system).

A good nonconformity statement has three parts: the requirement, the evidence found and why it does not meet the requirement. Example: “Requirement: the access control policy requires quarterly reviews of administrator accounts (Annex A 5.18). Evidence: no review record for Q1 and Q2 for the ERP. Nonconformity: the access review was not performed as required.” Without evidence there is no finding.
points: 9.1 what to measure, how, when, who analyses: evaluate performance and effectiveness.
9.2 internal audit programme covering all clauses and the scope; impartial auditors; ISO 19011 and ISO 27007.
9.3 management review with defined inputs and recorded decisions.
10.2 nonconformity: correct, find the root cause, corrective action, check effectiveness, record.
Finding = requirement + evidence + why it is not met.

Requirement   Access control policy section 4: quarterly review of ERP admin

Evidence      Review records exist for Q3 and Q4 2025; none for Q1 and Q2 2026

lessons.title: The road to certification
text: A first ISO 27001 project in a mid-sized organisation usually takes 6 to 12 months. The typical path is: get management support and a budget, define the scope, run a gap assessment against the clauses and Annex A, carry out the risk assessment and treatment, write the SoA and the missing policies and procedures, implement the controls, run the ISMS for a few months so that records exist, then perform an internal audit and a management review before the certification audit.

Certification is done by a certification body accredited by a national accreditation body (COFRAC in France, UKAS in the United Kingdom, DAkkS in Germany). The initial audit has two stages. Stage 1 reviews the documentation and readiness: scope, policy, risk assessment, SoA, internal audit and management review done, and plans stage 2. Stage 2, a few weeks later, checks on site or remotely that the ISMS is implemented and effective: interviews at all levels, sampling of records, observation of controls.

Auditors report major nonconformities (a requirement not met at all, or a failure that calls into question the ISMS’s ability to achieve its results, for example no internal audit or no risk assessment), minor nonconformities (a partial or isolated failure), observations and opportunities for improvement. Major nonconformities must be corrected and verified before the certificate is issued; for minor ones, the auditor accepts a corrective action plan.

The certificate is valid for three years. Surveillance audits take place in years one and two, shorter and focused on samples and on changes, and a recertification audit in year three. The ISMS must therefore live all year: risk updates, internal audits, management reviews and corrective actions are checked every time.

Common findings in a first certification are risk assessments that are not linked to the SoA, exclusions without real justification, internal audits that did not cover all clauses or were done by people auditing their own work, management reviews missing required inputs, no evidence of awareness or competence, suppliers not assessed, and access reviews or restore tests missing for some quarters. A GRC analyst who prevents these is very valuable.
points: Path: support and budget → scope → gap assessment → risks and SoA → controls → run → internal audit → management review → certification.
Accredited certification body (COFRAC, UKAS, DAkkS).
Stage 1: documents and readiness; stage 2: implementation and effectiveness.
Major nonconformity: fixed before certification; minor: corrective action plan accepted.
Three-year certificate, surveillance audits in years 1 and 2, recertification in year 3.

example.code:
Month  1    Management approval, scope, project team
Month  2    Gap assessment (clauses 4-10 and Annex A)
Month  3-4  Risk assessment and treatment, SoA, policies
Month  4-7  Implement missing controls, awareness, supplier reviews
Month  8    ISMS running: records, indicators, first committee
Month  9    Internal audit, corrective actions, management review

pitfalls: Treating Annex A as the whole standard: clauses 4 to 10 are what certification checks first.
Excluding controls in the SoA without a real justification.
A risk assessment that does not explain why each control was chosen.
Choosing a scope that leaves out an essential dependency.
Writing long procedures for the auditor that nobody follows.
Internal audits by people auditing their own work, or not covering every clause.
Stopping the ISMS after the certificate: surveillance audits check that it lives all year.

exercises.q: Match each ISO 27001 clause with its main topic.
pairs: Risk assessment, risk treatment and the SoA
Measurement, internal audit and management review
exercises.answer: Clauses 4 to 6 plan the ISMS, 7 and 8 run it, 9 checks it and 10 improves it: the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. Clause 8 (operation) applies the plans of clause 6.

exercises.q: Sort these Annex A controls into their theme.

groups.name: Organisational
items: Information security for use of cloud services

exercises.answer: Organisational controls are policies, roles and processes; people controls concern employees before, during and after employment; physical controls protect sites and equipment; technological controls are implemented in systems. Threat intelligence, cloud services, data leakage prevention and secure coding are among the 11 controls added in 2022.

exercises.q: What is the Statement of Applicability?
options: The certificate issued by the certification body
The list of every Annex A control with whether it applies, the justification and its implementation status
The list of laws that apply to the organisation
exercises.answer: The SoA is a mandatory document produced during risk treatment (clause 6.1.3). For each of the 93 Annex A controls, and any additional controls, it states applicability, the justification for including or excluding it, and whether it is implemented. Auditors and clients ask for it first.

exercises.q: How many controls does Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 contain?
exercises.answer: 93 controls: 37 organisational, 8 people, 14 physical and 34 technological. The 2013 version had 114 controls in 14 domains; the 2022 version merged and reorganised them and added 11 new ones.

exercises.q: Put the steps of a first certification project in order.
steps: Management approves the project and the scope
Gap assessment against the clauses and Annex A
Risk assessment, treatment plan and Statement of Applicability
Implement the missing controls and run the ISMS
Stage 1 audit by the certification body
Stage 2 audit by the certification body
exercises.answer: The scope and management support come first, the gap assessment shows the work to do, the risk treatment decides the controls, and the ISMS must run long enough to produce records. The internal audit and management review are required before the certification body’s stage 1 (documents) and stage 2 (effectiveness).

exercises.q: During stage 2, the auditor finds that no internal audit has ever been performed. How is this finding usually classified?
exercises.answer: A whole required process (clause 9.2) is missing, which calls the system’s ability to check itself into question: a major nonconformity. It must be corrected, with an internal audit actually performed and verified, before the certificate can be issued. One late or incomplete audit would more likely be minor.

exercises.q: In B7, compute the share of applicable Annex A controls that are fully implemented, as a decimal.
exercises.explain: 64 / 86 ≈ 0.74: about three quarters of the applicable controls are fully implemented. Divide by the applicable controls, not by 93, because excluded controls are not expected to be implemented. The 15 partial and 7 missing controls form the action plan.

exercises.q: You run the internal audit of the access control process. Walk through it.

steps.text: What do you prepare before the interviews?

choices.label: The requirements to check (policy, Annex A 5.15 to 5.18, 8.2, 8.5), the records to sample and an audit checklist
choices.feedback: Right: you audit against requirements, and you plan which evidence you will sample.

choices.label: Nothing: you will ask people what they do
choices.feedback: Without the requirements and a sampling plan, you cannot say whether what people do conforms.

choices.label: A list of the IT team’s mistakes you already know
choices.feedback: An audit is objective and based on evidence collected now, not on reputation.

steps.text: You sample 20 access requests: 18 are approved by the manager, 2 have no approval. What do you do?

choices.label: Record a finding with the requirement, the 2 cases as evidence and the gap, and ask why they happened
choices.feedback: Yes: a finding needs requirement, evidence and gap; understanding why prepares the root cause analysis.

choices.label: Ignore them, 90 % is good enough
choices.feedback: The policy requires approval for every access; 2 exceptions are a nonconformity to record, probably minor.

choices.label: Disable the 2 accounts yourself
choices.feedback: The auditor reports; correcting is the job of the process owner, otherwise you would later audit your own work.

steps.text: The process owner fixes the 2 cases. Is the nonconformity closed?

choices.label: Not yet: the cause must be found and a corrective action taken, then its effectiveness checked
choices.feedback: Right: the correction fixed the cases; clause 10.2 also requires a corrective action on the cause and a check that it works.

choices.label: Yes, the cases are fixed
choices.feedback: That is only a correction. Without a corrective action, the same gap will reappear.

choices.label: Yes, once the auditor signs the report
choices.feedback: Closure depends on evidence that the corrective action is effective, not on a signature.

exercises.answer: Prepare against requirements with a sampling plan, record findings as requirement, evidence and gap, leave the correction to the process owner, and close only after a corrective action on the root cause has been checked as effective.

exercises.q: Write the scope statement for an ISO 27001 project at a 50-person company that sells a single SaaS product, hosted on a public cloud.
exercises.hint: What is in, where, which teams and systems, interfaces with what is out.
exercises.answer: The information security management system covers the development, operation and support of the [product] SaaS platform and the personal and client data it processes. It includes the product, engineering, operations, support and IT teams, the production and pre-production environments hosted in the cloud provider’s EU regions, the source code and CI/CD pipeline, and the laptops and SaaS tools used by these teams, from the [city] office and remote work. Finance, sales and HR are outside the scope; their interfaces with the ISMS (onboarding and offboarding, contracts with clients and suppliers) are covered by documented procedures. The cloud provider is managed as a supplier under control 5.23, relying on its own certifications.

exercises.q: Write a nonconformity for this observation: the backup policy requires a restore test every quarter, but the last restore test record is 9 months old.
exercises.answer: Requirement: the backup policy (section 3) requires a quarterly restore test of the production database, in line with Annex A 8.13 Information backup. Evidence: the most recent restore test record is dated 14 January; no records exist for the following two quarters, and the IT operations lead confirmed no test was performed. Nonconformity: restore tests were not performed as required for two consecutive quarters, so the ability to recover the production database has not been verified. Classification: minor, since backups run and one test was performed this year. Expected response: correction (perform a restore test now), root cause analysis and a corrective action to prevent recurrence, for example scheduled tests with a named backup owner and monitoring in the security committee.

exercises.q: A client asks your company for its ISO 27001 certificate and SoA before signing. What do you check before sending them, and what do you send?
exercises.answer: I check that the certificate is valid, issued by an accredited certification body, and that its scope covers the service the client is buying; if not, I explain what is in scope. For the SoA, I check it is the current approved version. The SoA describes how we protect ourselves, so I send it under a non-disclosure agreement, or send a summarised version that lists the controls and their status without internal details such as system names or open weaknesses. I also offer the most relevant documents for their questionnaire, such as security policies summaries or the latest surveillance audit result, and a contact for further questions.

interview.a: An information security management system is the set of policies, processes, roles, risk assessments and controls by which an organisation manages information security and continually improves it. It is not a technical tool. ISO 27001 specifies the requirements for it in clauses 4 to 10, built on Plan-Do-Check-Act, and Annex A lists the controls to consider.

interview.q: What is the difference between ISO 27001 and ISO 27002?
interview.a: ISO 27001 contains the requirements an organisation is certified against: the management system clauses and the list of Annex A controls. ISO 27002 is guidance: for each control it explains the purpose and how to implement it, and gives attributes such as control type and security properties. You cannot be certified against 27002, but implementers and auditors use it all the time.

interview.q: Name a few of the controls that were new in ISO 27001:2022.
interview.a: There were 11, for example threat intelligence, information security for the use of cloud services, ICT readiness for business continuity, physical security monitoring, configuration management, information deletion, data masking, data leakage prevention, monitoring activities, web filtering and secure coding. They reflect cloud adoption, data protection and modern attack detection.

interview.q: What is a Statement of Applicability and why does it matter?
interview.a: It lists every Annex A control, says whether it applies, justifies the decision and gives its implementation status. It links the risk treatment to the controls, so it shows that the ISMS is based on the organisation’s risks. Auditors start with it, and clients often ask for it, so exclusions must have real justifications.

interview.q: How does a certification audit work?
interview.a: An accredited certification body performs a two-stage initial audit. Stage 1 reviews the documentation and readiness, such as scope, risk assessment, SoA, internal audit and management review. Stage 2 checks implementation and effectiveness through interviews, observation and sampling of records. Major nonconformities must be closed before the certificate is issued, minor ones need a corrective action plan. The certificate lasts three years with surveillance audits in the first two years and a recertification in the third.

interview.q: What is the difference between a correction and a corrective action?
interview.a: A correction fixes the specific problem found, for example disabling the account of a person who left. A corrective action removes the cause so that it does not happen again, for example automating account disabling from the HR system. Clause 10.2 requires both when relevant, plus a check that the corrective action was effective, and records of all of it.

interview.q: What are the most common findings in a first ISO 27001 audit?
interview.a: A risk assessment not clearly linked to the SoA, exclusions without justification, internal audits that did not cover all clauses or were not impartial, management reviews missing required inputs, no evidence of awareness or competence, suppliers not assessed, and periodic controls such as access reviews or restore tests missing for some periods. I prevent them by building records into each process and running a full internal audit early enough to fix gaps.
